name: Sushila
definition: Sushila is a composite portrait of a woman balancing seasonal factory work and household management in a coastal taluk of Uttara Kannada, where Gulf remittances and local processing industries shape family decisions about education and migration. She represents households caught between the promise of Karavali's high literacy rates and the daily pull of wage work and limited local opportunity.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Sushila works at a cashew processing unit near Kumta town, shelling and grading kernels during the peak season from February through June. The work pays roughly one hundred and eighty to two hundred rupees per day, though payment often arrives weeks late and depends on the quantity processed rather than hours worked. Outside the season she takes up piecework sorting dried fish or weeding coconut plots for neighbours. Her husband Prakash works as a driver for a timber merchant in Sirsi, home only on Sundays. The household runs on his monthly salary of about twelve thousand rupees plus her seasonal earnings. Cashew dust irritates her throat and the factory shed has poor ventilation, but the work is close enough to reach by bus under the Shakti scheme, saving the fare. Prices for raw cashew nuts have climbed and the merchant complains about competition from Vietnamese imports, making every season uncertain. She keeps a kitchen garden of greens and drumstick behind the house, and neighbours share jackfruit and mangoes when the trees bear. Daily meals centre on rice, coconut chutney, fish curry when affordable, and dhal. Prakash's timber-merchant employer sometimes delays salary during the monsoon when logging stops.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Sushila lives with her two sons, aged nineteen and fourteen, and her mother-in-law, who is in her seventies and manages the cooking when Sushila is at the factory. Her husband Prakash stays in a shared room in Sirsi during the week. Her elder son Suresh completed his second PUC last year at the government college in Kumta and now works at a mobile-phone shop in town, earning about seven thousand rupees a month while he prepares for the police recruitment exam. Her younger son Pradeep is in ninth standard at the government high school. Suresh's income helps but he is restless, talking about joining his maternal uncle in a hotel kitchen in Mumbai or trying for Gulf work through an agent in Bhatkal. Sushila's mother-in-law, widowed thirty years ago under the old Aliyasantana property customs that gave Billava women some holding rights, owns the small house plot and a share in an adjoining coconut garden, though the trees are old and yield little. Sushila's own mother lives in her brother's household near Honnavar. Housework, fetching water from the public tap during summer shortages, and looking after her mother-in-law's medicines for blood pressure fall to Sushila when she is not at the factory. Pradeep sometimes complains that his friends' families are building new houses with Gulf money while they remain in the old tiled house.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Sushila studied only until seventh standard in the village school near her childhood home, leaving when her family needed her labour in the fields and during the fishing season. She reads Kannada slowly and cannot follow English at all. Suresh and Pradeep both attended the government Kannada-medium school in Kumta; Suresh passed his SSLC with a second class and his PUC with lower marks, enough to keep the door open for a constable post but not for engineering or degree college without paying for private coaching the family cannot afford. Pradeep is a better student, ranking in the top fifteen in his class, and his teachers say he should aim for PUC science stream. The school is three kilometres from home; Pradeep cycles or takes the morning bus. There is no tuition cost under government schooling but books, uniforms, the bicycle repair and the PUC college fee of about three thousand rupees a year stretch the household budget. Sushila wants Pradeep to finish PUC and find a government job or join a diploma course, but Suresh's example worries her—two years of college and still no permanent job. Her husband talks about putting Pradeep into a hotel-work apprenticeship after tenth if no decent exam result comes, saying the Udupi-hotel network has built more family security than degrees. She resists but knows the pull of immediate earnings. She wishes Kumta had a private English-medium school they could afford, seeing how the doctor's and merchant's children speak confidence her sons lack.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Sushila's throat trouble from cashew dust worsens each season; she treats it with home remedies and occasional visits to the government primary health centre in Kumta, where the doctor gives an inhaler she uses sparingly to make it last. Her mother-in-law takes tablets for high blood pressure and diabetes, collected free under the government scheme at the taluk hospital, though the queues are long and the daughter-in-law must accompany her. Prakash injured his back two years ago lifting timber and still feels pain during the monsoon; he went once to a private clinic in Sirsi and paid fifteen hundred rupees for an X-ray and tablets but has not returned for follow-up. The family is enrolled under Ayushman Bharat but has never used the hospitalisation cover; serious cases from Kumta go to Karwar district hospital or, if one can pay, to Manipal, which feels impossibly far and expensive. Pradeep had dengue fever during the monsoon last year and recovered at home with paracetamol and boiled neem water. There is fear of snakebite during the rains when the fields flood and of monkey fever in the forest-edge villages, though Kumta town itself has been spared recent outbreaks. Sushila has not seen a dentist despite a nagging pain in one molar. Her mother-in-law's eyesight is failing and neighbours say cataract surgery is free under a government camp, but the old woman refuses to travel to Karwar. Sushila herself feels tired much of the time, a tiredness she attributes to age and work rather than illness.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Sushila's family belongs to the Billava community, historically associated with toddy-tapping and coconut cultivation, and now spread across many occupations in coastal Karnataka. She feels pride in the community's Koti-Chennaya oral epic and in the social mobility Billavas have achieved in the past generation. The family worships at the local Durgaparameshwari temple and participates in the annual Jatre, where Bhuta Kola performances invoke the daivas through the night. Her mother-in-law insists on specific offerings before the household deity each morning. Sushila respects these practices but does not share the older woman's intensity. Neighbours are a mix of Billava, Havyaka Brahmin, Mogaveera fishing families and a few Beary Muslim households; relations are civil though each community keeps to its own marriage and ritual circles. She has two close friends from the cashew factory, one Billava and one Mogaveera, with whom she shares complaints about wages and in-laws. The local Billava Sangha occasionally organises meetings about reservation policies and community welfare schemes, and her husband attends when he is home. Caste identity is spoken of openly here in a way that surprises visitors from cities. Sushila knows the GSB and Bunt families who own the larger cashew and trading businesses but has no social contact beyond the employer-worker relationship. During election seasons the community's leaders mobilise Billava voters and candidates promise attention to toddy-tappers' issues and labour rights, though Sushila sees little change.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Her mother-in-law draws an old-age pension of six hundred rupees per month, collected from the post office. The household has a ration card and receives rice and kerosene, though the quantities have shrunk and the shop sometimes runs out. Sushila applied for a toilets-construction grant years ago under the Swachh Bharat scheme but the funds never arrived and the family built a makeshift latrine with their own savings. She travels free on government buses under the Shakti scheme, a benefit she uses almost daily during the work season and considers the most tangible government help she has received. The gram panchayat is dominated by families with money and land; she has never spoken at a meeting. She hears of MGNREGA work but the going rate of two hundred and eighty rupees per day feels barely more than the cashew factory pays, and the work is irregular and requires forms she does not understand. Pradeep received a bicycle under a school scheme two years ago, which the family appreciated. When the timber merchant delayed Prakash's salary, the family had no one in the labour department to complain to and simply waited. Sushila is vaguely aware of Ayushman Bharat and other health schemes but finds the paperwork and hospital procedures intimidating. She trusts the anganwadi worker who visits her mother-in-law, less so the revenue officials who appeared once asking about property records she could not produce.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Sushila worries most about Suresh leaving for Mumbai or the Gulf before securing a stable future, fearing he will fall into debt to an agent or waste years in irregular work as so many boys from Kumta have done. She is proud that both her sons are literate and that Pradeep still attends school regularly, something she could not do, but she fears the education will lead nowhere without money for further study or contacts for a government job. She wishes Uttara Kannada had the opportunities that Mangaluru and Udupi offer—a medical college, an airport, the kind of private companies that hire steady workers—and resents that every ladder out of Kumta requires her sons to leave home. She blames the merchants who delay wages and the agents who lure boys with false promises of Gulf riches, and she blames a government she feels takes her vote and gives little back beyond the bus fare. She is proud of her ability to manage the household on a thin budget and of her mother-in-law's strength, and she takes satisfaction in the small respect neighbours give her for keeping her sons in school longer than many. She does not think caste discrimination has held her family back as much as simple poverty and geography, though she knows Brahmin and Bunt families command easier credit and better connections. She wants Pradeep to stay in school and finish PUC, then find any secure job with a pension, even a clerk's post. She demands nothing grand, only stability, a government hospital in Kumta that works without sending patients to Karwar, and an end to the cashew factory's wage delays.
